topic.name: Heart Failure
objectives: Distinguish HFrEF vs. HFpEF (systolic vs. diastolic failure)
Recognize clinical presentation: dyspnea, edema, JVD, rales
Order appropriate diagnostic tests (BNP, echo, CXR)
Know when to refer to cardiology or admit

lessons.title: 💔 Heart Failure 101: When the Pump Fails

content_chunks.title: Why This Matters
content_chunks.content: Meet Tom: 68, former trucker, type 2 diabetes, MI 5 years ago. He's been getting more short of breath walking to his mailbox. 'Getting old,' he figures. Then he wakes up gasping at 2 AM, has to sleep in his recliner. Shoes don't fit anymore—ankles are huge. This is classic heart failure. 6.2 million Americans have it, and it has a WORSE 5-year mortality than many cancers (50%). Early recognition = better outcomes.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Before/After comparison: LEFT: Normal heart pumping efficiently (EF 60%). RIGHT: Failing heart (dilated, EF 25%) with backup congestion to lungs and body

content_chunks.title: What IS Heart Failure?
content_chunks.content:
**Heart Failure (HF)**: The heart can't pump enough blood to meet the body's needs.

**Two Main Types**:

**HFrEF** (Heart Failure with **Reduced** Ejection Fraction)
• **EF <40%** (systolic dysfunction)
• Heart muscle is WEAK—can't squeeze properly
• Most common type (more treatment options)
• Main causes: MI, ischemic cardiomyopathy, dilated cardiomyopathy

**HFpEF** (Heart Failure with **Preserved** Ejection Fraction)
• **EF ≥50%** (diastolic dysfunction)
• Heart muscle is STIFF—can't relax/fill properly
• About 50% of HF cases now
• Main causes: HTN, diabetes, obesity, aging
• FEWER proven treatments (frustrating!)

**Key Point**: Same symptoms, different mechanisms, different treatments!
content_chunks.mnemonic: **rEF = wEak** (HFrEF = weak squeeze). **pEF = stIFF** (HFpEF = stiff muscle)
content_chunks.visual_desc: Side-by-side heart diagrams: LEFT (HFrEF): dilated, thin walls, weak contraction. RIGHT (HFpEF): thick walls, small chamber, can't relax

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **BNP/NT-proBNP** is your best friend for diagnosing HF! BNP >100 pg/mL or NT-proBNP >125 pg/mL = very likely HF. BNP <100 = HF unlikely (NPV >90%). Order it on everyone with unexplained dyspnea or edema!

mnemonics.mnemonic: **rEF = wEak** (HFrEF = weak squeeze). **pEF = stIFF** (HFpEF = stiff muscle)

quick_checks.q: Echo shows EF 35% with dilated LV. This is:
quick_checks.explanation: EF <40% = HFrEF (reduced/systolic failure). Heart is weak and can't squeeze effectively.

quick_checks.q: Best initial test to rule OUT heart failure in dyspneic patient?
quick_checks.explanation: BNP <100 has excellent negative predictive value (>90%) for ruling OUT HF. Much cheaper and faster than echo!

content_chunks.title: Classic Symptoms & Signs (Boards Gold)
content_chunks.content:
**Symptoms** (what patient tells you):
• **Dyspnea on exertion** (earliest symptom)
• **Orthopnea** (SOB lying flat - asks 'How many pillows?')
• **Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND)** - wakes up gasping at 2-3 AM
• **Fatigue** - can't do usual activities
• **Weight gain** (>2-3 lbs in 1 day or >5 lbs in 1 week = fluid overload!)

**Signs** (what YOU find):
• **Bilateral ankle edema** (pitting - press for 5 sec, leaves dent)
• **Crackles/rales** in lung bases (pulmonary congestion)
• **Elevated JVP** (jugular venous pressure >8 cm)
• **S3 gallop** ('Kentucky' - ventricular gallop, very specific for HF)
• **Hepatomegaly** (RV failure backs up into liver)
• **Ascites** (severe RV failure)

**Framingham Criteria**: Need 2 major OR 1 major + 2 minor to diagnose clinically
content_chunks.visual_desc: Human body diagram with arrows pointing to: lungs (rales), neck (JVD), heart (S3), liver (hepatomegaly), legs (edema)

content_chunks.title: NYHA Classification (Memorize This!)
content_chunks.content:
**New York Heart Association Functional Classes**:

**Class I**: HF present but NO symptoms with ordinary activity
• 'I feel fine!'

**Class II**: Slight limitation - comfortable at rest, symptoms with ORDINARY activity
• 'I get short of breath walking upstairs'

**Class III**: Marked limitation - comfortable at rest, symptoms with LESS than ordinary activity
• 'I get winded walking to the bathroom'

**Class IV**: Unable to do ANY activity without symptoms, or symptoms at REST
• 'I can't breathe just sitting here'

**Why it matters**: Guides treatment intensity and prognosis
content_chunks.mnemonic: **NYHA 1-2-3-4 = NO-ORDINARY-LESS-ANY**: Class **1** = **NO** symptoms, Class **2** = **ORDINARY** activity limited, Class **3** = **LESS** than ordinary, Class **4** = **ANY** activity or rest
content_chunks.visual_desc: Staircase diagram: Class I at top (walking upstairs easily), Class II (struggling on stairs), Class III (struggling on flat ground), Class IV (sitting in chair, struggling)

content_chunks.title: Diagnostic Workup
content_chunks.content:
✅ **BNP or NT-proBNP** - screening test, severity marker
• BNP >400 or NT-proBNP >450 = likely acute decompensation

✅ **Transthoracic Echo** - REQUIRED for diagnosis!
• Determines EF (HFrEF vs HFpEF)
• Assesses valves, wall motion, chamber sizes

✅ **Chest X-ray**
• Cardiomegaly (heart >50% thoracic width)
• Pulmonary edema (Kerley B lines, cephalization, pleural effusions)

✅ **ECG**
• Look for: MI, LVH, arrhythmias (AFib common!)

✅ **Labs**
• **BMP**: Check renal function (Cr, GFR), electrolytes
• **CBC**: Anemia can worsen HF
• **TSH**: Hyperthyroid can cause high-output HF
• **Lipid panel**: CAD risk
• **Troponin**: Rule out ACS if acute presentation

✅ **Consider coronary angiography** if ischemic cause suspected (most common!)
content_chunks.visual_desc: Diagnostic flowchart: Suspect HF → BNP + CXR + ECG → Echo (definitive) → Labs → Determine cause

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **S3 gallop** = 'Ken-TUC-ky' (3 sounds). **S4** = 'TEN-nes-see' (4 sounds, heard in HTN/stiff ventricle). S3 is VERY specific for volume overload/HF. If you hear it, think fluid!

mnemonics.mnemonic: **NYHA 1-2-3-4 = NO-ORDINARY-LESS-ANY**: Class **1** = **NO** symptoms, Class **2** = **ORDINARY** activity limited, Class **3** = **LESS** than ordinary, Class **4** = **ANY** activity or rest

quick_checks.q: Patient has dyspnea climbing stairs but fine at rest. NYHA class?
quick_checks.explanation: Class II = symptoms with ORDINARY activity (like stairs). Comfortable at rest.

quick_checks.q: Which finding is MOST specific for HF diagnosis?
quick_checks.explanation: S3 gallop is highly specific for volume overload/HF. Other findings are sensitive but less specific.

content_chunks.title: HFrEF: The 'Fantastic Four' (GDMT)
content_chunks.content:
**Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy** for HFrEF (ALL patients need these unless contraindicated!):

**1️⃣ ACE-I or ARB** (or ARNI)
• **Goal**: Block harmful remodeling, ↓mortality 20-30%
• **Examples**: lisinopril 5-40 mg daily, sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto)
• **Monitoring**: Cr, K+ at 1-2 weeks (tolerate Cr increase <30%, K+ <5.5)

**2️⃣ Beta Blockers** (specific ones only!)
• **Approved**: carvedilol, metoprolol succinate (NOT tartrate!), bisoprolol
• **Goal**: ↓mortality 30%, prevents remodeling
• **Start low, go slow** - can worsen HF initially
• **Pearl**: Start AFTER diuresis (never in acute decompensation)

**3️⃣ Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonists (MRA)**
• **Examples**: spironolactone 12.5-25 mg, eplerenone
• **Use if**: NYHA Class II-IV with EF ≤35%
• **Watch**: Hyperkalemia (K+ >5.5 = stop), gynecomastia (spironolactone)

**4️⃣ SGLT2 Inhibitors** (NEW in 2022!)
• **Examples**: dapagliflozin 10 mg, empagliflozin 10 mg
• **Goal**: ↓HF hospitalization 30%, works in HFrEF AND HFpEF!
• **Bonus**: Also great for diabetes

**The Goal**: Start ALL four classes! Mortality drops 50-75% with full GDMT vs. none.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Four pillars holding up 'Survival' platform: ACE-I/ARB, Beta Blocker, MRA, SGLT2i

content_chunks.title: Diuretics: Symptom Relief
content_chunks.content:
**Loop Diuretics** (for congestion/edema):
• **Examples**: furosemide (Lasix) 20-240 mg daily, bumetanide, torsemide
• **Goal**: Remove excess fluid, improve symptoms
• **DON'T improve mortality** (unlike GDMT above)
• **Monitoring**: Daily weights, K+, Mg++, Cr

**When to use**:
• Start when patient has volume overload (edema, rales, JVD)
• Titrate to **euvolemia** (dry weight, no edema)
• Once stable, can often reduce or stop

**Patient education**:
• Weigh daily (same time, same scale)
• If weight ↑ 2-3 lbs in 1 day or 5 lbs in 1 week → call provider
• Low-sodium diet (<2g/day)
content_chunks.clinical_pearl: Loop diuretics make patients FEEL better but don't make them LIVE longer. GDMT (ACE-I, BB, MRA, SGLT2i) does both!

content_chunks.title: When to Admit vs. Manage Outpatient
content_chunks.content:
**ADMIT if** (acute decompensated HF):
• Hypoxia (O2 sat <90%)
• Respiratory distress
• Hypotension (SBP <90)
• Acute kidney injury
• Troponin elevation (ACS)
• Arrhythmia (new AFib, VT)
• Refractory symptoms despite outpatient treatment

**Outpatient management** if:
• Mild volume overload
• Stable vital signs
• Adequate diuresis possible with oral meds
• Good follow-up available
• Patient reliable

**Follow-up**: See in 1-2 weeks after new diagnosis or med change
content_chunks.visual_desc: Decision tree: Acute HF presentation → Check O2, BP, renal function → Unstable = ADMIT, Stable = Outpatient with close follow-up

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **HFpEF treatment is LIMITED**: No proven mortality benefit from ACE-I/ARB or beta blockers. DO use: diuretics for symptoms, SGLT2i (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin - proven!), and treat underlying causes (HTN control!). Main goal = manage comorbidities.

mnemonics.mnemonic: **ARBS** save lives: **A**CE-I/**ARB**, **R**eceptor blocker (beta), **B**lockade of aldosterone (MRA), **S**GLT2 inhibitor

quick_checks.q: Which med improves symptoms BUT NOT mortality in HFrEF?
quick_checks.explanation: Loop diuretics (furosemide) improve congestion/symptoms but don't reduce mortality. GDMT meds (ACE-I, BB, MRA) do both!

quick_checks.q: Patient with new HFrEF (EF 30%). Which beta blocker?
quick_checks.explanation: Only 3 beta blockers proven in HF: carvedilol, metoprolol SUCCINATE (ER), bisoprolol. NOT tartrate (immediate release)!

quick_checks.q: HFpEF patient. Which med has PROVEN mortality benefit?
quick_checks.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) are the ONLY meds with proven benefit in HFpEF! Game-changer in 2022.
